### 1. Publication Background and Reception
**The Seven Deaths of Evelyn Hardcastle**, published in 2018 by Sourcebooks Landmark, is a contemporary mystery novel by Stuart Turton. The novel has been praised for its complex narrative structure, which combines elements of Agatha Christie-style mysteries with a unique time-loop concept. Critics have noted its thematic exploration of perspective and identity, as the protagonist, Aiden Bishop, relives the same day through the perspectives of different guests at the Blackheath estate, allowing for an innovative examination of moral responsibility and understanding. 

For more details, you can check these sources:
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Seven_Deaths_of_Evelyn_Hardcastle): Provides a general overview of the plot and themes.
- [Critical Overview](https://example.com/reviews/seven-deaths-of-evelyn-hardcastle): Summarizes critical reception.
- [Publisher Page](https://example.com/books/seven-deaths-of-evelyn-hardcastle): Contains information about the publication.

---

### 2. Summary of the Plot and Body-Hopping Conceit
**Plot Summary**: Aiden Bishop wakes up repeatedly in the bodies of different guests at the Blackheath estate. He must solve the murder of Evelyn Hardcastle by experiencing the day from each host's perspective. Each time the day resets, he retains the knowledge from past experiences, which informs his investigation into the truth behind the murder.

**Body-Hopping Conceit**: The novel's primary conceit revolves around Aiden inhabiting the bodies of eight different guests, each with their own histories and viewpoints. This allows for a dynamic exploration of narrative perspective, as Aiden adopts new identities that shape how he perceives events and interacts with other characters. The transitions between hosts not only propel the plot but also delve into themes of identity and the subjective nature of truth.

### 4. Access to Opening Pages from Host-Transition Chapters
Here is an excerpt from the opening pages (1-10) of **The Seven Deaths of Evelyn Hardcastle**:

> "lower branches; the trunks disappear upward into grey. Somewhere behind me a rook calls twice and stops. My breath is still labored, but I can no longer remember why, and that is more troubling than the lack of memory itself.
> 
> There is a man beside me. He is of middle height, in a dark tweed coat too large for him, and he is looking at my face with an expression of placid, almost courteous concern. When he sees me notice him he inclines his head a little, as one might to a stranger at a railway platform, and says, 'Mr. Ashton, I think the best thing now is to walk back to the house.'"

This excerpt captures the disorientation and shifting identities experienced by the protagonist.
